title_en: Against the Letter of Mani Called Fundamental
author: Augustine of Hippo
addressee: Manichaeans (and in part the Manichaean correspondent Patticus, addressed within Mani's letter)
occasion: Augustine, a former Manichaean, refutes the opening of Mani's 'Letter of Fundamental Principles,' which Manichaeans treated as a foundational text, to show that its claims are false and that its promised certain knowledge is never delivered.
argument: Augustine first explains why he remains in the Catholic Church: its authority, universality, and succession from the apostles, which alone moved him to believe the gospel. He then examines the opening of Mani's Fundamental Letter, showing that Mani cannot prove he is an apostle of Christ or the promised Paraclete, and that his promise of certain knowledge collapses into a demand for blind faith. Augustine argues that Mani's account of two eternal substances, the land of light and the land of darkness, is incoherent and even blasphemous, since it imagines God as a bodily mass extended through space and penetrated by evil. Finally, he argues that evil is not a nature but corruption, that all natures insofar as they exist are good, and that corruption arises not from God but from the fact that creatures were made from nothing.

outline.move: Augustine prays to God for a peaceful mind, seeking the correction of Manichaeans rather than their destruction.
He contrasts himself with those who rage against Manichaeans, describing the difficulty of overcoming carnal fantasies and the long process of spiritual healing.
Augustine gives his autobiographical account of having been deceived as a Manichaean, explains why he cannot rage against them, and asks that both sides set aside arrogance and seek truth together.

He states what holds him in the Catholic Church—its universal consent, authority, and succession—and argues that he believes the gospel only because the Catholic Church commends it, so Manichaeans cannot use the gospel to persuade him.

Augustine examines Mani's self-designation as 'apostle of Jesus Christ' and argues that Mani cannot show he was sent or assumed by the Holy Spirit, and that his avoidance of the title 'apostle of the Paraclete' reveals pride and deceit.
Augustine discusses the Manichaean celebration of Mani's death-day (the Bema) instead of Christ's passion, arguing that Mani denied Christ's true birth and passion to promote his own commemoration.
He shows from the Acts of the Apostles that the Holy Spirit was already sent at Pentecost, so Mani cannot claim to be the Paraclete.

Augustine notes that Mani's opening promises of salvation and certain knowledge are mere promises, and that Mani then proceeds to tell incredible stories about a battle before the constitution of the world.
He quotes Mani's description of the land of light and asks how Mani could know these things, arguing that Mani demands belief in uncertain things after promising certain knowledge.

Augustine argues that God is not a body extended through space, using the nature of the soul—its presence as a whole in every part of the body, its memory, and its power to judge images—to show that spiritual realities are not spatial.

He examines Mani's claim that the land of darkness lay 'beside one side' of the land of light, showing that this implies both are bodies and that the resulting picture of God is deformed and blasphemous.

Augustine asks whether the Father, his kingdoms, and the land of light are one substance or many, and argues that Mani is forced either to admit that God's own nature is penetrated by darkness or to admit that God made the land of light from nothing.
He considers the possible shapes of the two lands' adjoining sides and argues that any configuration produces absurdities.

Augustine uses the example of the rectitude of the land of darkness's side to argue that evil is not a substance but the corruption or loss of form in a substance, and that even the land of darkness contains goods that must come from God.

Augustine examines the five natures of the land of darkness and their inhabitants, arguing that their order, form, life, and health are goods that cannot be attributed to anything but God, and that Mani's account is based on careless observation of this world.

He argues that if the evils Mani names are removed, good natures remain, but if the goods are removed, no nature remains; therefore every nature, insofar as it is a nature, is good, and evil is corruption, not a nature.
Augustine explains that corruption arises because creatures were made from nothing, not from God, and that God justly orders even corruption for punishment and correction.
He supports this with Scripture, showing that God is said to 'corrupt' or 'destroy' the wicked, and argues that corruption tends toward non-being, while being comes from God.
Augustine concludes by urging his readers to seek the incorruptible good through purity of heart, and to reject Mani's heresy, which disfigures the divine substance by spreading it through space.

cast.name: Mani
cast.who: Founder of Manichaeism, author of the Fundamental Letter, who claimed to be an apostle of Jesus Christ and the Paraclete.

cast.name: Patticus
cast.who: The correspondent addressed in Mani's letter, who asked about the birth of Adam and Eve.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle, cited by Augustine for his apostolic call and history in Acts, and for 1 Corinthians 3:17 on God's punishment of those who corrupt his temple.

cast.name: Theophilus
cast.who: The addressee of the Acts of the Apostles, mentioned in Augustine's quotation of Acts.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first man, whose birth Patticus asked about.

cast.name: Eve
cast.who: The first woman, whose birth Patticus asked about.

voices.speaker: Mani (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'inquit' or similar verbs of saying, and quoted directly from the Fundamental Letter.

voices.speaker: Manichaean interlocutor (imagined)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'inquit' or 'dicis' as an objection Augustine anticipates.

voices.speaker: Scripture (quoted)

The Holy Spirit promised by Christ; Mani claimed to be this Spirit.

The doctrine that God made creatures from nothing, not from his own substance or from pre-existing matter.

scripture: Augustine quotes the Old Testament from Latin versions based on the Septuagint, and the New Testament from Old Latin versions. He refers to the Acts of the Apostles as 'the Acts of the Apostles' and quotes it alongside the Gospel. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint/Latin tradition. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and, where applicable, note the Septuagint Psalm numbering.
uncertain: The precise date of composition is not stated in the text; 396-397 AD is a common scholarly estimate.
The identity of Patticus beyond being the addressee of Mani's letter is not established in the source.
Whether Augustine quotes the Fundamental Letter verbatim throughout or paraphrases in places cannot be fully determined from the source alone.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul, source_forms: ["Paulus"], who: The apostle, cited by Augustine for his apostolic call and history in Acts, and for 1 Corinthians 3:17 on God's punishment of those who corrupt his temple.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul is not mentioned in the source text. The reference to 1 Corinthians 3:17 in section 39 is introduced as 'apostolus Paulus adtestatur' but the name 'Paulus' does not appear in the source text provided; the reference is to 'apostolus Paulus' in the biblical quotation context, but this exact form is not in the source. More importantly, the source does not mention Paul's apostolic call and history in Acts as claimed—Acts discusses Paul's conversion but Augustine does not cite this in the provided text.

Section 2 contains no direct scripture quotation; it contains Augustine's own reflections with biblical allusions (e.g., 'ortus est mihi iustitiae sol' and 'erat lumen uerum') but these are not introduced as formal quotations with 'scriptum est' or similar markers. Section 37 contains no direct scripture quotation in the provided text. The brief should list sections 1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 39, 42 for direct scripture quotations, or clarify that sections 2 and 37 contain allusions rather than formal quotations.

Section 10 does not contain an imagined Manichaean interlocutor; it is Augustine's own argument about the Holy Spirit's coming. Section 37 does not contain an imagined Manichaean interlocutor; it is Augustine's direct address to the rational soul ('natura animae rationalis'). Section 41 does not contain an imagined Manichaean interlocutor; it is Augustine's own argument using the analogy of voice and silence. The brief should list sections 20, 30, 32, 34 for the imagined Manichaean interlocutor, or clarify the marking more precisely.

The source uses 'Euae' (genitive of Eva), not 'Eva' as a source form. The brief's 'names' object should use 'Euae' as the source form, or the cast entry should note that 'Eva' is a reconstructed nominative form not directly appearing in the text.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Augustine first explains why he remains in the Catholic Church: its authority, universality, and succession from the apostles, which alone moved him to believe the gospel.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: tenet consensio populorum atque gentium; tenet auctoritas miraculis inchoata, spe nutrita, caritate aucta, uetustate firmata; tenet ab ipsa sede Petri apostoli... usque ad praesentem episcopatum successio sacerdotum; tenet postremo ipsum catholicae nomen
_unresolved_facts.fix: Augustine explains what holds him in the Catholic Church in section 4, but the argument that this 'alone moved him to believe the gospel' overstates the case. Augustine says 'euangelio non crederem, nisi me catholicae ecclesiae conmoueret auctoritas' (section 5), but this is part of a specific argument about why he cannot accept Mani's claims, not a general statement that the Church's authority alone moved him to believe. The brief should clarify that this is part of an epistemic argument about authority, not a biographical claim about his conversion.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["6", "7"], move: Augustine examines Mani's self-designation as 'apostle of Jesus Christ' and argues that Mani cannot show he was sent or assumed by the Holy Spirit, and that his avoidance of the title 'apostle of the Paraclete' reveals pride and deceit.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 7 does not examine Mani's self-designation as 'apostle of Jesus Christ'; rather, it extends the argument from section 6 by asking why Manichaeans fear to believe in Christ's birth from a virgin while accepting that Mani was 'assumed' by the Holy Spirit. The focus shifts to the Incarnation and the virgin birth as a comparative argument. The brief should clarify that section 7 applies the logic of section 6 to the specific case of Christ's birth versus Mani's origin.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["9", "10"], move: He shows from the Acts of the Apostles that the Holy Spirit was already sent at Pentecost, so Mani cannot claim to be the Paraclete.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 10 does not focus on showing from Acts that the Holy Spirit was sent at Pentecost; rather, it argues that the Spirit was given twice (after the Resurrection and at Pentecost) based on John 20:22 and Acts 2, and then returns to Augustine's methodological stance of seeking to learn rather than teach. The Pentecost argument is primarily in section 9. The brief should clarify that section 10 adds the Johannine post-Resurrection gift of the Spirit and discusses method, while section 9 contains the main Pentecost argument.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["15", "16", "17", "18", "19"], move: Augustine argues that God is not a body extended through space, using the nature of the soul—its presence as a whole in every part of the body, its memory, and its power to judge images—to show that spiritual realities are not spatial.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 15 does not use the nature of the soul to argue that God is not a body; it quotes Mani's description of the land of darkness and then begins a digression on whether God could be an aerial or aetherial body. The soul argument begins in section 16. The brief should note that section 15 sets up the problem with Mani's corporealism and contains a brief argument about divine incorporeality, while sections 16-19 contain the extended soul argument.

_unresolved_facts.claim: section ["26"], move: He considers the possible shapes of the two lands' adjoining sides and argues that any configuration produces absurdities.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 26 does not argue that 'any configuration produces absurdities'; rather, it argues that the most plausible configuration (straight sides adjoining) produces the most harmonious and beautiful result, which paradoxically undermines Mani's claim that the land of darkness is summum malum. Augustine's point is that even in the land of darkness there is rectitude (a good), and that the configuration shows concord and peace rather than the hostility Mani describes. The brief should clarify that section 26 uses reductio to show that the land of darkness contains goods, not merely to show geometrical absurdities.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["36", "37", "38"], move: Augustine explains that corruption arises because creatures were made from nothing, not from God, and that God justly orders even corruption for punishment and correction.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 37 does not focus on explaining that corruption arises because creatures were made from nothing; rather, it addresses the question of why God did not make all things 'summe bona' and discusses the hierarchical ordering of goods, the unique generation of the Son, and the rational soul's need to accept its place in the hierarchy. The 'made from nothing' argument is primarily in sections 36 and 38. Section 37's main contribution is the argument about hierarchical goods and the soul's pride. The brief should redistribute: section 36 introduces creation from nothing; section 37 discusses the hierarchy of goods and the rational soul; section 38 returns to corruption and divine ordering.
